characters.note: A pictograph — the oracle-bone form already looks like flowing water ripples, making it one of the clearest characters to trace through the whole evolution.
The oracle-bone form shows three peaks side by side; after the regular script, the peaks simplify into a symmetrical vertical-stroke pattern.
The oracle-bone form is a circle with a dot at its center; after seal script it squares off into a rectangle.
The oracle-bone form is a crescent moon, contrasting with 日's path toward a squared-off shape.
The oracle-bone form shows raindrops falling beneath a sky canopy; after the clerical-script transformation the drops regularize into four dots.
Originally a pictograph of swirling cloud vapor; a rain radical was later added to form 雲, and the simplified script restores the original form.
The oracle-bone form shows a flickering flame; the strokes straighten and become symmetrical through the clerical-script transformation.
A pictograph of a tree, branches above and roots below; the structure has stayed stable for thousands of years.
Looks like a field crossed by raised paths — a classic example of early script standardization.
The oracle-bone form emphasizes the mane and four legs; after the 1956 simplification the four legs collapse into a single stroke — one of the most symbolized simplifications.
The oracle-bone form takes the frontal silhouette of an ox's head with its two horns; later forms keep the horns and simplify the rest.
Shares the same head-and-horns approach as 牛, making the two characters' evolutions instructive to compare.
The oracle-bone form traces the fish's whole body; after the clerical-script transformation the tail simplifies into four dots.
The early forms are winding and highly varied — a strong example of a pictograph becoming a highly abstract symbol.
Shares an origin with 隹; its form has split and merged between a literal bird and a radical over time.
The oracle-bone form is a person standing in profile — the simplest, most direct character in the whole evolution.
The oracle-bone form shows a kneeling figure with clasped hands; that sense of posture fades gradually in later forms.
The oracle-bone form is a swaddled infant, with an oversized head and swinging arms especially prominent.
The oracle-bone form is an eye drawn on its side; later scripts turn it upright into a rectangular frame.
The oracle-bone form outlines a heart; it later became a highly productive radical for abstract meanings.
The oracle-bone form details the carriage box, wheels, and axle — one of the most heavily simplified characters.
A pictograph of two facing door panels; the shift from traditional 門 to simplified 门 shows both continuity and rupture in the same evolution.
A pictograph of a curved blade in profile, already compact and efficient in its earliest form.
Taken from the side profile of a tool, gradually abstracted into the two-horizontal-one-vertical symbol it is today.
Early scholarship reads the form as resembling an axe or halberd, a symbol of authority; the three-horizontal-one-vertical structure was fixed in later scripts.
From 或 (a halberd guarding a territory) to 國 and then simplified 国 — its evolution is intertwined with the changing idea of a state.
A pig under a roof — this image of domestic life has barely changed in thousands of years.
The oracle-bone form shows a woman seated safely beneath a roof; that sense of ease and comfort survives into the modern character.
Formed from 日 (sun) and 月 (moon); its structure has changed little over millennia even as its meaning grew more abstract.
Formed from 人 (person) and 言 (speech) — from the concrete idea of a person standing by their word to an abstract, semantic value.
